Block-print tradition
Place & origin

A specialist centre on the Krishna coast.

Machilipatnam / Pedana Kalamkari belongs to the Krishna-coast textile tradition. Krishna District’s ODOP material identifies Pedana as a specialist centre and describes production in Pedana and neighbouring villages around Machilipatnam.

This page stays focused on the block-printing ecosystem of Machilipatnam and Pedana. It does not collapse the distinct Srikalahasthi freehand tradition into the same process.

Regional trade-history context

Andhra cloth was travelling long before QVibe.

Museum collections and textile history document painted and dyed cottons from India’s Coromandel Coast made for overseas markets during the 17th and 18th centuries.

QVibe is not inventing the idea of cloth from this coast travelling beyond India. The modern question is different: how can today’s craft travel while its place, process and identity remain visible?

More than one product

A language already living in many forms.

Krishna District’s official ODOP overview identifies several forms. The craft already exists beyond a single product category; these are examples of its present language, not QVibe inventory.

QVibe exploration

Where could the language travel next?

The objective is not to make Kalamkari “western”. It is to explore new contexts while keeping the craft recognisable as itself.

QVibe & Kalamkari

Let pattern keep its provenance.

QVibe wants to document the living block-print ecosystem, understand what makers already sell successfully and explore how stronger provenance and presentation may help the craft travel without becoming anonymous pattern.
